questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.learningObjective: Recognize the shape of a normal distribution
questions.stem: Meteorologist Eli notes daily highs are bell-shaped and symmetric. Which distribution fits?
questions.explanation: A bell-shaped symmetric continuous distribution is normal. Uniform is flat, exponential is skewed.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the sampling distribution of the sample mean
questions.stem: Eli takes many samples of size 30 and computes their means. What is the distribution of those means?

options.text: Always exactly normal regardless of population
Approximately normal by the central limit theorem

options.misconception: confuses sample mean with individual values

questions.explanation: By the CLT, sample means are approximately normal for large n. It is not exact for small n or non-finite variance.

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.stem: Eli tests whether a storm model is broken. A type I error means?

options.text: Failing to detect a broken model
Declaring the model broken when it is fine

questions.explanation: Type I error is rejecting a true null, i.e., a false positive. Type II is a false negative.

questions.stem: Eli asks what power means for his storm test. Which is correct?

options.text: Probability of rejecting a false null

questions.explanation: Power = P(reject H0 | H0 false). It is 1 minus type II error probability.
questions.hint: Probability of detecting a real effect.

questions.stem: Eli's temperature 85, mean 70, sd 5. What is the z-score?

questions.topic: The standard error of a mean
questions.stem: Eli's sample sd 4, n 16. What is the standard error of the mean?
questions.explanation: SE=sd/sqrt(n)=4/4=1.

questions.stem: Eli reports 95% CI for mean temp (68,72). Correct interpretation?

options.text: We are 95% confident the true mean is in (68,72)
There is 95% probability the mean is in this interval
options.misconception: treats interval as random after construction

questions.explanation: The CI expresses confidence in the method, not a probability about a fixed interval or data range.

questions.stem: Eli gets p=0.03 for a storm effect. What does it mean?

options.text: Probability of data this extreme if null is true

questions.explanation: A p-value is P(data this extreme | H0 true), not P(H0 true) or effect size.
questions.hint: Assuming null, how extreme is data.

questions.stem: Eli tests for a rare storm event with a 99% accurate detector. A positive result likely means?

options.text: Possibly a false positive due to low base rate

questions.explanation: With a rare base rate, even a 1% false positive rate can dominate, so a positive may be a false positive.

questions.stem: Eli tests whether mean temp equals 70. What is H0?
questions.explanation: H0 is the status quo equality claim. The alternative is that the mean differs or exceeds.

questions.stem: Eli uses alpha=0.05 and gets p=0.07. What is the decision?

options.misconception: confuses fail to reject with accept

questions.explanation: When p>alpha, fail to reject H0. Failing to reject is not proving H0 true.

questions.stem: Eli's residual plot shows a U-shaped curve. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: A curved pattern in residuals indicates the linear model misses a nonlinear trend.
questions.hint: Pattern in residuals signals model issue.

questions.stem: Eli plots wind speed vs power output and sees a curve flattening at high speed. Relationship?
questions.explanation: A flattening curve is nonlinear. Nonlinear does not mean no relationship.

questions.stem: Eli's residuals fan out as predicted values increase. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Fan-shaped residuals indicate changing variance, i.e., heteroscedasticity.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.learningObjective: Compute percentage within 2 sd for normal
questions.stem: Eli's normal rainfall: mean 100, sd 15. About what percent within 2 sd?
questions.explanation: Empirical rule: about 95% within two standard deviations.

questions.learningObjective: Compute standard error for a mean
questions.stem: Eli's population sd 12, sample size 36. What is the standard error?

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.stem: Eli asks what a type II error is. Which is correct?

options.text: Failing to reject a false null

questions.explanation: Type II error is a false negative: failing to reject H0 when it is false.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a way to increase power
questions.stem: Eli wants more power for his storm test. Which helps?
questions.explanation: Larger sample size reduces standard error and increases power. Raising alpha also raises power but at cost of type I errors.

questions.stem: Eli's rainfall 130 mm, mean 100, sd 15. What is z?

questions.topic: The standard error of a mean
questions.learningObjective: Explain effect of sample size on SE
questions.stem: Eli doubles his sample size. What happens to standard error?
questions.explanation: SE=sd/sqrt(n). Doubling n multiplies denominator by sqrt(2), so SE divides by sqrt(2).

questions.stem: Eli's z*=1.96, SE=2. What is the margin of error?
Eli gets p=0.001. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A small p-value indicates strong evidence against H0. It does not imply large effect size or bias.
questions.hint: Small p = strong evidence against H0.

questions.stem: Eli: storm base rate 0.01, detector true positive 0.99, false positive 0.05. What is P(storm | positive)?
Eli tests H0: mu=70 vs Ha: mu≠70. Which is the alternative?
questions.explanation: The alternative is mu≠70, a two-sided claim. Equality is the null.
questions.hint: Alternative is the claim we seek evidence for.

questions.stem: Eli uses alpha=0.05 and gets p=0.01. Decision?

options.misconception: confuses fail to reject with accept

questions.explanation: When p<alpha, reject H0. This indicates statistically significant evidence against the null.

questions.stem: Eli's residual plot shows random scatter around zero. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Random scatter suggests linearity and constant variance are plausible. It does not prove correctness.

questions.stem: Eli sees a curved relationship. Which approach can help linearize?

options.text: Apply a log or square-root transformation

questions.explanation: Transformations like log or square root can linearize curved relationships. Removing data is invalid.

questions.stem: Eli has heteroscedastic residuals. Which remedy is common?

options.text: Use weighted least squares or transform y

questions.explanation: Weighted least squares or transforming the response can stabilize variance. Ignoring it affects inference.
questions.hint: Stabilize variance via weighting or transform.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: Eli's normal data: mean 0, sd 1. Approximate z for the 97.5th percentile?
questions.explanation: The 97.5th percentile of standard normal is about 1.96.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability sample mean exceeds a value
questions.stem: Eli: population mean 100, sd 20, n 25. What is P(sample mean > 108)? z for 108 is 2.

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.learningObjective: Tradeoff between type I and type II
questions.stem: Eli lowers alpha from 0.05 to 0.01. What happens to type II error?
questions.explanation: Lowering alpha makes rejection harder, increasing type II error (and decreasing power).

questions.stem: Eli increases effect size. What happens to power?
questions.explanation: Larger effect size is easier to detect, so power increases. It does not automatically reach 1.

questions.stem: Eli's temp mean 70, sd 5. What value corresponds to z=2?
questions.explanation: value=mean+z*sd=70+2*5=80.

questions.topic: The standard error of a mean
questions.learningObjective: Compute SE with known population sd
questions.stem: Eli's population sd 8, n 64. What is SE?
Eli: sample mean 75, SE 3, z*=1.96. What is the lower bound of 95% CI?

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a p-value is not
questions.stem: Eli says p=0.2 means there is 20% chance H0 is true. Is that correct?

options.text: No, p is not P(H0 true)

questions.explanation: A p-value is not the probability that H0 is true. It assumes H0 true and measures data extremity.

questions.stem: Eli's detector is 99% accurate for a rare storm. Explain why base rate matters for interpreting a positive.

answer.exemplar: Even with high accuracy, a rare base rate means false positives can outnumber true positives, so the posterior probability of a storm given a positive may be surprisingly low.

questions.explanation: Base rate neglect leads to overestimating posterior probability. Bayes' theorem incorporates the base rate.

questions.stem: Eli tests whether mean temp is greater than 70. What is Ha?
questions.explanation: The alternative matches the research claim: mu>70. Equality is the null.

questions.stem: Eli tries many models until p<0.05. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Searching until significance is p-hacking, inflating false positives. Power analysis and validation are different.

questions.stem: Eli's residual spread increases with fitted values. What problem is this?
questions.explanation: Increasing spread with fitted values is heteroscedasticity, violating constant variance.

questions.stem: Eli sees a clear curve in scatterplot. Does that mean no relationship?

options.text: No, there is a strong nonlinear relationship

questions.explanation: A curve indicates a nonlinear relationship, not absence of relationship. Linear is not the only kind.

questions.stem: Eli ignores heteroscedasticity. What is affected?

options.text: Standard errors and inference are unreliable

questions.explanation: Heteroscedasticity does not bias coefficients but makes standard errors unreliable, affecting inference.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: Eli's normal data mean 50, sd 10. About what percent below 70?
questions.explanation: 70 is 2 sd above mean. About 97.5% below (50%+34%+13.5%).

questions.stem: Eli has n=5 from a skewed population. Can he rely on CLT?

options.text: No, small n from skewed population is risky
Yes, CLT works for any n

questions.explanation: CLT needs sufficiently large n, especially for skewed populations. n=5 is too small to rely on it.

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.stem: Eli's test has power 0.8. What is P(type II error)?
questions.explanation: Type II probability = 1 - power = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2.

questions.learningObjective: Explain effect of alpha on power
questions.stem: Eli raises alpha from 0.05 to 0.10. What happens to power?
questions.explanation: Higher alpha makes rejection easier, increasing power but also type I error rate.

questions.stem: Eli: city A temp 80 (mean 70, sd 5), city B 90 (mean 75, sd 10). Which is more unusual?
questions.explanation: z_A=(80-70)/5=2, z_B=(90-75)/10=1.5. City A is more unusual (higher |z|).

questions.topic: The standard error of a mean
questions.stem: Eli estimates proportion 0.4 with n 100. What is SE of proportion?
Eli wants a narrower CI. Which helps?
questions.explanation: Larger n reduces SE and narrows CI. Higher confidence or sd or smaller n widens it.

questions.stem: Eli gets p=0.04 with alpha=0.05. Explain the decision and its limitation.

answer.exemplar: Since p=0.04 is less than alpha=0.05, reject H0. However, this does not prove the alternative is true or measure effect size; it only indicates incompatibility with H0.

questions.explanation: Reject H0 when p<alpha. Significance is not proof or effect size.

questions.stem: Eli: base rate 0.02, test sensitivity 0.95, false positive 0.1. What is P(disease | positive)?
Eli fails to reject H0. Can he conclude H0 is true?

options.text: Yes, failure to reject proves H0
options.misconception: confuses fail to reject with accept

options.text: No, because H0 is always false
No, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence

questions.explanation: Failing to reject does not prove H0 true; it only means insufficient evidence against it.
questions.hint: Fail to reject is not proof.

questions.stem: Eli uses a two-sided test. What does the p-value measure?

options.text: Probability of deviation at least as extreme in either direction
Probability of deviation in one direction

questions.explanation: Two-sided p-value covers extreme deviations in either direction. It is not P(H0 true) or effect size.

questions.stem: Eli sees one residual far from the rest. What should he do?

options.text: Investigate for data error or special cause

questions.explanation: An outlier residual warrants investigation for errors or special causes, not automatic deletion or ignoring.

questions.stem: Eli's scatterplot shows a U-shape. Which model may fit better?
questions.explanation: A U-shape suggests a quadratic term. Removing the predictor loses information.

questions.stem: Eli has heteroscedasticity but wants to keep the model. Which adjustment helps inference?
questions.explanation: Robust standard errors adjust inference under heteroscedasticity without changing the model.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.learningObjective: Apply empirical rule to a real context
questions.stem: Eli's normal temps mean 60, sd 5. About what percent between 50 and 70?
questions.explanation: 50 to 70 is mean ±2 sd, about 95% by empirical rule.

questions.learningObjective: Compute CI for a mean with known sd
questions.stem: Eli: sample mean 20, population sd 4, n 16, z*=1.96. Margin of error?

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.learningObjective: Explain type I/type II tradeoff in context
questions.stem: Eli lowers alpha to reduce false storm alarms. Explain the tradeoff.

answer.exemplar: Lowering alpha reduces type I errors (false alarms) but increases type II errors, meaning real storms may be missed. The tradeoff depends on the costs of each error.

questions.explanation: Lower alpha reduces false positives but increases false negatives. Costs determine the choice.

questions.stem: Eli wants to increase power. Explain which factors help.

answer.exemplar: Power increases with larger sample size, larger effect size, and higher alpha, but higher alpha also raises type I errors. Better measurement reduces variability too.

questions.explanation: Power depends on n, effect size, alpha, and variability. Tradeoffs exist with alpha.
